segments.text: Inside a banana, tiny black specks line up in a row.
Turns out, those are seeds that never got to grow.
Wild bananas used to be packed with big, hard seeds.
The bananas we eat have one extra set of chromosomes than normal.
To make a seed, chromosomes need to pair up two by two.
But since it's an odd number, one always gets left out.
So instead of a real seed, only a trace is left behind.
Instead of seeds, a shoot from the roots gets cut and replanted.
Every banana grown that way shares the same genes.
So the bananas we eat today are basically all clones.
